name: PT Bank Nationalnobu Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank Nationalnobu: a fee-led small bank priced for permanent disappointment
frontmatter.summary: NOBU's fee line was never a bet on the QRIS merchant discount rate: micro merchants already paid zero, so extending zero MDR removes almost none of the revenue behind the earnings surprise, and we hold the nine-month run-rate into FY2026E. The shares instead discount a bank that permanently under-earns its cost of equity; the book anchor is the unaudited third-quarter figure, capital closes the tier gap from retained earnings, and normalised returns support a value well above the price.
thesis: The fee engine is real and was never MDR-dependent: micro merchants already paid no merchant discount rate on small QRIS tickets before the October 2026 change, so extending zero MDR to all merchant categories leaves the revenue that multiplied the fee line broadly intact - our base case keeps fee growth positive, decelerating with volume rather than price.

Asset quality looks strong on the ratio card but low-quality loans are 8.9% of the book and nine-month provisioning ran well below the FY2025 charge; we model a through-cycle credit cost above both recent years.

Capital is the real constraint: core capital (modal inti) of RpIDR4,381.1bnbn is well above the current floor but below the level the KBMI I category implies, and the model reaches the higher tier on retained earnings without new shares in FY2029E - which is why dilution sits in our bear case, not our base.

The shares trade at 0.6x book and 4.1x earnings; on a normalised 11.0% return on equity against a 12.45% cost of equity, warranted P/BV is 0.83 times book, so the discount - not growth - is the return.
Liquidity is the reason the discount can persist: free float is 7.3% and turnover is thin, so position sizing, not valuation, is the binding risk for most holders.

blocks.text: We initiate on Bank Nationalnobu (NOBU) with a **BUY** rating and a target of **Rp561**, 49.3% above the Rp376 close. This is a small-cap bank that compounded net profit from RpIDR141.5bnbn in FY2023 to RpIDR481.3bnbn in FY2025 and passed that full-year figure in the first nine months of 2026 alone, and it now trades at 0.6x book and 4.1x earnings [S0, S2, S3].

The market is not wrong that something broke, but the cause we can source is capital and control, not the payments rule. Profit growth was carried by non-interest income - fees and commissions rose from RpIDR269.0bnbn in FY2024 to RpIDR469.3bnbn in FY2025 and RpIDR628.4bnbn in 9M2026 - built on QRIS merchant acquiring through more than 2.0 m merchantsm merchants and 143 k agentsk agent-banking points [S3, S5]. The rule that took effect on 1 October 2026 extends the zero merchant discount rate to tickets of up to one hundred thousand rupiah at every merchant category, but micro merchants already paid zero on tickets up to five hundred thousand rupiah under the earlier concession [S10]. For an acquirer whose base is micro merchants with small tickets, the change removes almost no revenue that was being earned; what it removes is the rest of the industry's pricing power on the smallest tickets. Layer on the collapse of the proposed merger with Bank MNC, which OJK had required because neither bank met the minimum core capital rule, and the de-rating from a one-year high of RpRp710 to RpRp368 becomes explicable [S6].

Our variant view is narrower than "cheap bank". We do not argue that NOBU deserves a growth multiple. We argue that the market has moved from pricing a fee-led compounder to pricing a bank that permanently earns less than its cost of equity, and that the second proposition is too harsh. The book we anchor on is RpIDR4,686.7bnbn of equity at 30 September 2026, which is unaudited; the last audited anchor is FY2025 equity of RpIDR4,168.3bnbn, and the valuation section carries the target on audited book as a stated sensitivity [S2, S3]. Capital adequacy sits at 24.7%, and even after normalising credit costs above both recent years and decelerating the fee line from FY2027E, the model earns a return on equity of 13.1% in FY2027E and 11.0% by FY2030E, against a cost of equity of 12.45% [S2, S3]. A bank earning close to its cost of equity is worth close to its book; the shares are at 0.6x of it.

Three things move the value. First, whether the merchant franchise keeps acquiring customers as fast as it did in the nine months to September - we hold that run-rate for FY2026E and then model fee income compounding with volume, not with pricing, which from FY2027E is a slower line than the run-rate [S10]. Second, the credit cost: we model 0.8% rising to 0.9%, above the FY2025 charge, because low-quality loans at 8.9% of the book have not yet been tested and the allowance covers only part of the impaired-stage pool [S2, S3]. Third, capital: a dilutive raise at a discount to book would transfer value from minority holders to the controlling shareholders, and there is a track record of exactly that. Our base case does not need one, because retained earnings carry core capital past the KBMI I ceiling in FY2029E.

The bear case is worth RpRp269 and the bull case RpRp889; probabilities of 25%, 50% and 25% give the blended target [S0]. The asymmetry is genuinely wide because the starting multiple is so low, but the thin float means few holders can express it at size: three-month average daily turnover is RpIDR2,416,384,266.7bn against a market capitalisation of RpIDR2,811,894,906,024.0bn.

NOBU is a commercial bank whose licence dates from 1990, when it operated as Bank Alfindo; it became a foreign-exchange bank in 2014 and has been listed on the IDX since its 2021 IPO [S9]. It reports through corporate and treasury segments and describes a franchise built on three legs: consumer, UMKM (micro, small and medium enterprises) and medium-to-large commercial lending [S9]. The consumer leg includes home mortgages and personal loans; the commercial leg is a working-capital book; and the treasury operation runs a sizeable securities and repo book that is visible in the balance sheet rather than in the segment narrative [S3].

The distinguishing asset is not the loan book but the payments and agency network. Nobu has built a merchant-acquiring business on QRIS - it reported more than a million merchants at end-2024 and more than 2.0 m merchantsm merchants plus 143 k agentsk agent-banking points at end-2025 - working through aggregator partners such as PT Order Kuota Evolusi Digital, whose agent networks sit in the informal retail economy [S5, S9]. That network generates merchant fees, account and float balances, and a pipeline for micro lending: micro and retail loans reached RpIDR1,300.0bnbn at end-2024, growing 40.0%, funded through direct lending, channeling to peer-to-peer lenders and BPRs, and products such as KRUPUK and the Kasbon Suka-Suka paylater pilot [S9].

The balance sheet at 30 September 2026 shows how unusual the mix is for a bank of this size. Gross loans were RpIDR24,779.9bnbn against customer deposits of RpIDR9,648.2bnbn of demand deposits, RpIDR1,907.8bnbn of savings and RpIDR19,362.6bnbn of time deposits, with a loan-to-deposit ratio of 80.2% [S2]. The rest of the asset side is a treasury book, funded in part by securities sold under repo of RpIDR7,849.5bnbn [S2]. Earning assets of RpIDR39,371.3bnbn at end-2025 materially exceeded the loan book, which matters for the interest margin: NOBU partly runs a carry trade, not purely a lending spread [S3].

Ownership is the second defining feature. At 31 December 2025 the controlling shareholders were Hanwha Life Insurance of Korea and PT Putera Mulia Indonesia, with the ultimate controlling shareholders named as Seung Youn Kim and James Tjahaja Riady [S3]. Hanwha acquired 40.0% of the paid-up capital from Lippo-affiliated holders - PT Putera Mulia Indonesia, PT Prima Cakrawala Sentosa, PT Multipolar, PT Star Pacific, PT Inti Anugrah Pratama, PT Ciptadana Capital and PT Lenox Pasifik Investama - in a transaction announced in January 2025 [S4]. The consideration was disclosed only at nominal value, so the transaction gives us the size and identity of the buyer but not an arm's-length price per share [S4]. The Lippo relationship is visible operationally: branches sit in Lippo malls and plazas across the country, and the bank's buildings are insured with PT Lippo General Insurance [S3, S9]. A Korean strategic holder alongside an Indonesian conglomerate gives the bank capital and bancassurance reach, but it also means minority holders own a small slice of a company whose strategy is set between two controlling groups: free float is 7.3% [S0].

Strategy has been consistent for five years: use digital payments and agent banking to acquire mass-market customers cheaply, convert them into depositors, then lend to them at micro and consumer yields. The capital history tells the cost of that strategy - the share count went from 4,952.2m to 7,478.4m through rights issues, and the FY2024 annual report refers to a second and third rights issue to strengthen its position in the KBMI I capital group [S0, S9].

Indonesia's banking system is large, profitable and structurally under-penetrated in credit, and the competitive hierarchy is brutal for small banks. The large state-linked and private groups dominate low-cost deposits; below them sit second-tier private banks with niche franchises; at the bottom sit the KBMI I banks with core capital up to IDR6.00tn, of which NOBU is one [S11]. The regulator has been explicit that it wants fewer, better-capitalised banks: OJK required NOBU and MNC's Bank to explore a merger in 2023 because neither met the minimum core capital requirement, wrote formally to every KBMI I bank in late October 2025 asking it to evaluate its capital and consolidation options, and after the parties abandoned the transaction in November 2025 asked both controlling shareholders to keep strengthening capital directly or to invite strategic investors [S6, S11]. That is the single most important industry fact for this name: capital, not demand, determines who can grow, and deleting the KBMI I category would push the effective floor to the boundary of the next tier [S11].

The macro backdrop is mildly supportive for margins and unsupportive for the currency. The house macro deck holds the BI policy rate at 5.8 rate, CPI at 3.3 rate and real GDP growth at 5.3 rate, with the rupiah projected at Rp18,350/USD against the dollar by FY2027E. A flat policy rate means deposit competition does not ease much: funding costs reprice only as fast as the deposit mix allows, and NOBU's deposit mix improved over the nine months rather than deteriorated - demand deposits and savings both grew faster than time deposits, lifting the CASA share of deposits [S2]. The reported net interest margin for the first nine months of the year was 3.6%, below the level the full FY2025 accounts produced, and the cause sits on the asset side: loan yields in a micro and merchant market where fee income has been competed away and the contest has moved into the lending rate [S2, S3, S10]. Small banks with a small CASA base are still the first to be squeezed if rates turn sticky, exactly as the bank method card warns, but the compression here is a yield story, not a funding-mix story.

Payments is where the industry story intersects this company, and the detail matters more than the headline. QRIS has become the country's default retail rail, and zero MDR is not new: Bank Indonesia has long applied a zero merchant discount rate to micro (UMi) merchants on tickets of up to five hundred thousand rupiah, and in August 2026 it extended zero MDR to transactions of up to one hundred thousand rupiah across all merchant categories, effective 1 October 2026 [S10]. The intent is to widen acceptance and cut transaction costs for merchants at the smallest ticket sizes. The consequence for acquirers is two-sided: the micro-merchant business that an agent-network bank can reach was already earning no MDR, so the change takes pricing away from the rest of the industry rather than from NOBU, while the volume effect runs the other way. Value in this rail has to come from float, account fees and lending, which is the cross-sell Nobu describes - the right strategic answer, but a slower revenue line than pricing power [S9, S10].

Competitive position: NOBU is a challenger, not a leader. It has no meaningful share of system loans and its deposits are small against the large banks; its edge is speed in micro-merchant onboarding through partners, and its weakness is the absence of a low-cost deposit franchise. We assess the moat as thin but not zero. Switching costs on the merchant side are low - a merchant can accept QRIS from any acquirer - so the network is defensible only through service and agent economics; on the lending side, micro underwriting at scale is a genuine capability, but the loan book is young and has not been through a full credit cycle [S2, S3, S9].

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power (depositors) is high and rising, because time deposits and repo are price-takers and the CASA base is small. Buyer power (borrowers) is moderate: micro borrowers pay up for access, but the bank competes with peer-to-peer lenders and BPRs that are not bound by the same capital rules. New entrants are a real threat in payments, where fintechs and e-wallets compete for the same merchants without a banking balance sheet. Substitutes are strong in deposits - money-market funds and digital savings products - and weak in micro credit. Rivalry is intense at the bottom of the market and essentially absent at the top, because NOBU cannot compete for large corporate relationships [S2, S3, S9].

Regulation is the swing external influence: the zero-MDR extension [S10], the KBMI capital escalation and OJK's formal letters to KBMI I banks [S11], and the merger policy that first forced and then released consolidation [S6]. Governance and disclosure matter too, and we treat the failed merger as information: a transaction designed to solve a capital problem was abandoned, which leaves the capital question to the controlling shareholders.

The history is one of rapid balance-sheet growth with a changing mix. Total assets went from RpIDR26,622.4bnbn to RpIDR33,325.8bnbn and RpIDR41,215.5bnbn, with gross loans of RpIDR20,184.9bnbn rising to RpIDR24,236.5bnbn and deposits of RpIDR24,393.3bnbn to RpIDR28,969.6bnbn [S3]. Net interest income grew from RpIDR735.8bnbn to RpIDR992.9bnbn and RpIDR1,134.2bnbn, but the driver was volume rather than spread: on our definition - net interest income over average productive assets - FY2025 was 3.2%, and the reported margin had slipped to 3.6% by the third quarter of 2026 as time deposits and repo replaced cheaper funding [S2, S3].

Non-interest income is where the story is. Fees and commissions other than from loans grew from RpIDR269.0bnbn in FY2024 to RpIDR469.3bnbn in FY2025 and RpIDR628.4bnbn in the first nine months of 2026, taking total other operating income from RpIDR154.3bnbn in FY2023 to RpIDR290.4bnbn and RpIDR492.7bnbn [S3, S2]. This is the merchant and agency franchise monetising, and it is why earnings per share rose 46.3% in FY2025 while the balance sheet grew more slowly. Our forecast does not extrapolate it, and it does not cut it either: we hold the nine-month run-rate to the year end, which is FY2026E non-interest income of RpIDR849.4bnbn, then grow it at 10.0% in FY2027E and decelerate towards 6.0% by FY2030E [S2, S10]. Holding the run-rate is the sourced choice: no published figure quantifies a fourth-quarter step-down, and the 1 October 2026 rule removes almost no fee the bank was being paid, so cutting Q4 on that rule would be a default haircut rather than a forecast. The rule is the reason for the deceleration, not for a decline, and it caps fee growth at volume rather than at the rate printed in the first nine months [S10].

Costs have grown with the network. Operating expenses were RpIDR745.8bnbn in FY2024 and RpIDR879.2bnbn in FY2025, and in the first nine months of 2026 personnel costs alone rose sharply as the agent and merchant footprint expanded [S3, S2]. The cost-to-income ratio was 54.0% in FY2025 by our calculation against the bank's own 51.4% for 9M2026, and we hold it near 51.0% rather than assume the network scales for free: costs keep growing with the footprint even in the years when revenue growth is slower.

Credit quality is the part of the story that looks best and deserves the most scepticism. Gross NPL was 0.6% at 30 September 2026 with net NPL lower still, and impairment charges of RpIDR69.3bnbn in nine months were well below the FY2025 charge [S2, S3]. The ratio card also shows low-quality loans - performing but special-mention and restructured - at 8.9% of the book, a multiple of reported NPL [S2]. The audited accounts show what sits behind that: at 31 December 2025 the allowance was RpIDR238.5bnbn, just under one per cent of gross loans, of which RpIDR29.7bnbn covered the impaired (stage three) loans of RpIDR107.9bnbn and the balance covered the performing-but-watchlist (stage two) loans of RpIDR841.2bnbn [S3]. Coverage of the impaired bucket is therefore thin, and the watchlist stock is where a migration would come from. Either the underwriting is genuinely conservative and those loans cure, or the NPL ratio is flattered by restructuring that has not yet migrated. We take the through-cycle view the bank method card requires: the FY2025 charge was 0.6% of average loans, the 2026 run-rate is below it, and we model 0.7% rising to 0.9% - above both recent actual years, because a book growing at nine per cent needs a flow above the last two years' level to hold a stock ratio near one per cent while the special-mention pool migrates [S2, S3].

Capital and funding are adequate in ratio terms and constrained in level terms, and the distinction matters. Book equity was RpIDR4,686.7bnbn at 30 September 2026 on the unaudited quarterly statements, against audited FY2025 equity of RpIDR4,168.3bnbn, and the regulatory capital stock is smaller again: modal inti was RpIDR4,381.1bnbn, all of it common equity tier-one capital at a 23.6% ratio, with the difference to book equity made up of intangibles and prudential deductions [S2, S3]. Total capital stood at a KPMM of 24.7%, which clears the IDR3.00tn minimum core capital requirement; but OJK is preparing to delete the KBMI I category, whose ceiling is IDR6.00tn, and has told KBMI I banks to find capital or find a partner [S6, S11]. The arithmetic that matters is therefore the core-capital line, not the equity line: on the model's retained-earnings path book equity reaches RpIDR6,244.9bnbn in FY2028E and RpIDR7,006.0bnbn in FY2029E, and applying the same deductions leaves core capital below the ceiling in FY2028E and above it in FY2029E, without issuing a share [S2]. That is why the base case models no rights issue: the gap is closable from earnings inside three years, and the earlier raises were needed to meet a floor the bank had breached, not to fund growth [S9]. Payout stays at zero until that crossing and then starts at 20.0% in FY2029E and 20.0% in FY2030E, the level the retained-earnings identity payout = one minus growth over return on equity permits at a constant capital ratio against 9.0% loan growth and an FY2030E return on equity of 11.0% - a distribution funded by growth-consistent retention rather than by releasing the capital buffer, so CAR is held roughly flat rather than drawn down. The identity at 4.0% terminal growth would permit a much higher payout, but we do not pay it: that would slow the core-capital build below the ceiling the regulator is moving to, so the 20.0% path is the deliberate one and the DDM is capitalised on it rather than on the higher terminal identity. The capital story here is comfortable ratios, a binding absolute floor that earnings close in FY2029E, and a dividend that starts only once the capital stops being needed.

Earnings quality flags, run in the order the house card requires. Accruals are not meaningful for a bank; the equivalent test is provisioning versus write-offs, and here the trend is the concern rather than the level - charges fell while low-quality loans stayed flat at 8.9% and the allowance covers only part of the impaired and watchlist pools, a divergence flag we resolve by modelling a higher charge, not by assuming a clean book [S2, S3]. Receivables and inventory tests do not apply. There is no IDX special-monitoring notation or special letter in the market data we hold, and the stock passes our board and liquidity screens on that basis, though turnover is thin [S0]. Related-party gravity is modest on the loan side - RpIDR292.6bnbn of related-party loans against a RpIDR24,236.5bnbn book - but related-party deposits of RpIDR2,535.1bnbn are a larger share of funding and fell year on year, which cuts both ways: less dependence on the group, but less stable funding [S3]. Structure flags: a controlling shareholder that is itself an insurer with a bancassurance agenda, a history of repeated rights issues, a small free float, and a failed related consolidation. None of these is a manipulation-class flag; they are optics-class and dilution-class flags, and we carry them as a discount to the multiple rather than as a reason to avoid the name.

We value NOBU on residual income and warranted P/BV, the house method for banks, with a dividend discount model as a floor and no weight on peer multiples because the listed comparables are either far larger or structurally different institutions. Residual income carries three fifths of the weight, warranted P/BV a fifth as the cross-check against traded book, and the DDM the remaining fifth [S0]. We moved weight out of warranted P/BV this round for a structural reason: the method takes a single sustainable-ROE point, so at a half weight it would put the same value into base, bear and bull alike and misprice both tails, whereas residual income discounts each scenario's own profit and equity path. For a bank, book value is the anchor - equity is marked and regulated, though the 30 September 2026 figure is unaudited and FY2025 is the last audited one - and the question is only what return the bank earns on it relative to what shareholders require.

The cost of equity is 12.45%, and the build is not the textbook one. The engine starts from the ten-year rupiah sovereign yield of 7.45%, deducts the Indonesia default spread the deck carries (1.62%), applies a beta of 0.90 to the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.23% plus the country risk premium of 2.46%, and adds an explicit company premium of 0.60% [S0]. Deducting the default spread at the risk-free rate and restoring only a beta-scaled country premium inside the equity premium leaves the total premium over the sovereign below the house IDR band, so the explicit premium is added to bring the cost of equity to the band floor - it is the house test applied rather than a discretionary add-on, and it also charges for a name with a 7.3% float and no published research coverage. We do not go above the floor: the country premium is already inside the build, and liquidity is carried explicitly below rather than hidden in the discount rate. The cost of the correction is real - the target falls from the below-band build we published first to RpRp561 - and it is the right price to pay for a denominator a reader can reproduce.

Primary method. Residual income starts from the 30 September 2026 book of RpIDR4,686.7bnbn, adds the present value of each forecast year's profit above the cost of equity charge on opening book, and capitalises the final year's excess return at 4.0%; it lands at RpRp572 [S0, S3]. This is the leg that carries the target, and it carries it because it is scenario-consistent: the bear run's own lower terminal return and its diluted share count are inside its number, and the bull run's higher return is inside its own.

The warranted P/BV cross-check, at a fifth of the weight, uses a normalised return on equity of 11.0% against a cost of equity of 12.45% and terminal growth of 4.0%, giving 0.83 times book, or RpRp522 [S0, S3]. The normalised return is the level our forecast converges to at FY2030E (11.0%), not the arithmetic mean of the first three forecast years, which would embed the FY2026E peak of 15.1% in perpetuity; the build behind it is the model's own steady state - a net interest margin of 3.1% on productive assets of about 1.56 times loans, a cost-to-income ratio of 52.0%, a cost of risk of 0.8% and leverage near eight times equity. It is deliberately held at a fifth and not a half: because the number is a single point, the multiple is 0.83 times book in every scenario, and weighting it heavily would flatten exactly the scenario dispersion the probability-weighted target depends on. It is shown so a reader can compare it with the traded 0.6x book.

The book value per share the cross-check is built on is the 30 September 2026 figure - equity of RpIDR4,686.7bnbn over 7,478.4m shares - which is unaudited [S2, S3]. The sensitivity that matters is the audited anchor: on FY2025 equity of RpIDR4,168.3bnbn, book value per share is Rp557, and the same 0.83 times multiple scales down in proportion to the lower book. That is the downside case on the book, not a forecast: the third-quarter LK is the most recent disclosure of the capital we are asked to value, and the FY2026 audit will settle it. The residual income model, which also starts from the unaudited book, is exposed to the same mark and we state it once rather than adjust the target for a risk the auditor has not flagged.

The DDM is the floor. It values the shares at RpRp181, -65.4% below the warranted P/BV cross-check, and that gap is above the house divergence threshold, so it needs an argument rather than a footnote: a bank that has never paid a dividend and only starts at 20.0% in FY2029E cannot be valued on its dividend stream today, and the divergence measures the value of retained earnings, which reaches shareholders only if the capital is not subsequently raised again at a discount [S0, S9]. The DDM is capitalised on the 20.0% payout the model actually pays in FY2030E, not on the higher payout the retention identity would allow at terminal growth, because the lower path is the one the capital position supports; a reader who lifted the payout to the identity would get a materially higher DDM, and we treat that as upside we have not underwritten. At the market price the shares are on 4.1x FY2026E earnings and 0.6x book, against an FY2026E return on equity of 15.1% and an FY2027E return on equity of 13.1% - a valuation that assumes either the equity is impaired or the return never recovers [S0].

The reverse test is the useful one. At RpRp376 the market capitalises NOBU at RpIDR2,811,894,906,024.0bn against FY2026E book of RpIDR4,849.5bnbn: at 0.6x book, with a 12.5% cost of equity and 4.0% terminal growth, the Gordon identity implied ROE = (P/BV) x (COE - g) + g resolves to a durable return in the high single digits - above the 7.4% sovereign yield but well below the cost of equity we charge, and far below the 15.1% we forecast. The gap to our number is therefore either a permanently lower return or a capital raise at a deep discount that dilutes today's book. We can construct that world - it is our bear case at RpRp269 - but it requires credit costs to run at the top of the industry range, the fee line to stall at its FY2026E level, and the controlling shareholders to solve the capital question by issuing stock at a discount rather than by retaining earnings for three years. The bull case, at RpRp889, requires the opposite: merchants convert into deposits and borrowers, fee income compounds at double digits, and capital above the floor is returned to holders.

The corporate-action option. The thesis does not rest on a takeover, but a control transaction is the fastest route to value and it deserves a price rather than a shrug. At one times the 30 September 2026 book the equity is worth RpIDR4,686.7bnbn against a market capitalisation of RpIDR2,811,894,906,024.0bn, and the strategic holder already owns 40.0% of the shares after buying out the founding group's affiliates [S4]. We do not put it in the probability-weighted target for two sourced reasons: no transaction is pending, and the one reference point we have - the Hanwha purchase - was disclosed at nominal value only, so there is no arm's-length per-share price to mark against and any multiple we chose would be invented [S4]. The failed MNC merger also shows how long consolidation takes to close and how easily it dies [S6]. It sits in the bull case, which is where the re-rating path lives, and it is the reason we would not dismiss the name on a weak fee quarter.

Excess capital is not yet available, which is the answer to the obvious question about a bank at 0.6x book. At a common equity tier-one ratio of 23.6% NOBU looks heavily over-capitalised, but the binding constraint is the absolute core-capital level rather than the ratio: modal inti of RpIDR4,381.1bnbn is above the IDR3.00tn floor and below the IDR6.00tn KBMI I ceiling that deleting the category would impose [S2, S6, S11]. A buyback at a discount to book would be strongly accretive per share, and it is exactly what the model cannot express in the base case - it would push core capital back below the ceiling the tier change implies at the moment the regulator is asking for the opposite. The model reaches the ceiling on retained earnings in FY2029E, after which the payout line starts at the identity-consistent 20.0% and is held there through FY2030E rather than rising to the higher payout the terminal identity would allow. The bull case, not the base, is where a buyback appears.

Finally, liquidity, which is the constraint the valuation cannot fix. Free float is 7.3% and three-month average daily value is RpIDR2,416,384,266.7bn, so the house liquidity table - which steps its target haircut in bands set by average daily value - gives no discount here, and the engine applies none. That is a statement about what the model can price, not about what a fund can hold: at this turnover a position large enough to matter to a diversified portfolio takes weeks to build and to exit, and the 49.3% is achievable only in a position the daily value supports. We would size this as a small position and would not treat the target as a liquid exit [S0].

The dominant risk is capital, not payments. OJK wrote to every KBMI I bank in late October 2025 asking for a review of capital and consolidation options, has said it intends to delete the KBMI I category, and told the shareholders of both NOBU and MNC Bank to inject capital or bring in a strategic investor after the merger failed; the likelihood is high and the impact on minorities is high, because the cheapest way to close a core-capital gap at a price below book is to issue shares [S6, S11, S4]. Our base case closes the gap from retained earnings inside two years, and the bear case models the alternative - a discounted issue that adds shares faster than it adds earnings, which is the largest single downside in the scenario set.

The payments risk is real but far smaller than the market appears to price. The zero merchant discount rate on tickets of up to one hundred thousand rupiah now applies to all merchant categories from 1 October 2026, but micro merchants were already at zero on tickets up to five hundred thousand rupiah, so the direct revenue loss to a micro-merchant acquirer is close to nil [S10]. What the rule removes is future pricing power on the smallest tickets, so the risk sits in the growth rate of the fee line rather than in its level: if merchants churn or onboarding slows, the fee line stalls at the FY2026E level instead of compounding, which is the bear's fee shock. The dominant second-order risk is competitive rather than regulatory - in an industry where nobody earns MDR on small tickets, the competition moves to float and credit, and the largest banks can fund that contest longer than a KBMI I bank can [S10, S9].

Macro and funding risks are moderate but persistent. Deposit competition from large banks and digital savings products keeps repricing the time-deposit book, and the model already embeds a thinner margin; a stronger rupiah or an easing cycle would help, a weaker one hurts because part of the deposit book is foreign currency [S3]. Commodity exposure is not direct - this is a domestic lender - so the house deck's caution on rate-sensitive Indonesian names is the relevant tilt, and it is part of why we do not ascribe a premium multiple.

Operational and franchise risks are the ones that are hard to price. The merchant network runs through third-party aggregators such as Order Kuota, so NOBU's customer relationship sits behind a partner that could be approached by a competitor [S9]. The micro and channeling book - RpIDR1,300.0bnbn of micro and retail loans at end-2024, plus exposure to peer-to-peer lending partners and BPRs - is young, and the low-quality loan ratio at 8.9% says the first test of that underwriting is still ahead [S2, S9].

Governance risk is a dilution risk. A controlling group that has funded growth through repeated rights issues, and a strategic shareholder that bought its 40.0% stake from the group rather than in the market, can solve a capital problem in ways that are value-accretive for the controller and dilutive for the minority [S4, S9]. We do not assume that happens; we note that the price already partly reflects it.
Liquidity risk is holding risk: with a 7.3% float and thin turnover, an investor who is right about the value may still not be able to trade the position at the price they believe [S0].

Signposts that would change our view: a dividend declaration at the FY2026 AGM (bullish for the DDM and for capital discipline); a fee line that holds flat or grows in the first two quarters after the MDR change (our bear case fails); low-quality loans migrating into NPLs above the FY2025 charge (bear); a rights issue at a price near or below current book (bear, and a governance event); an OJK-approved strategic transaction with a stronger institution (bull, and the re-rating trigger the market is waiting for).

Control sits with Hanwha Life Insurance, which holds 40.0% of the paid-up shares after buying out Lippo-affiliated holders in 2025, alongside PT Putera Mulia Indonesia, with Seung Youn Kim and James Tjahaja Riady named as the ultimate controlling shareholders [S3, S4]. The practical consequence is that the free float is 7.3% and insiders hold 46.1%, so the public shareholder base is small and the stock is a controlled company in all but legal form [S0]. We found no disclosure of pledged controlling shares in the filings and annual report extracts we archived; that is an absence of evidence, not evidence of absence, and it is a gap we will close at the next annual report [S3, S9].

Related-party dealings are disclosed and, on the lending side, small: loans to related parties of RpIDR292.6bnbn against a loan book of RpIDR24,236.5bnbn at end-2025, with deposits from related parties of RpIDR2,535.1bnbn [S3]. The insurance of the bank's buildings with Lippo General Insurance is a further disclosed relationship [S3]. The risk is less in these balances than in the direction of travel: a group that owns the controlling stake also owns the ecosystem the bank lends into, and the bancassurance relationship with Hanwha is both the strategic case and the conflict.

The dividend record is a governance fact in itself. The shares have not paid a dividend in any year covered by the price history, and the FY2024 annual report leaves the decision to the annual general meeting without a stated payout ratio [S0, S9]. For a bank earning near its cost of equity with capital well above the regulatory minimum, that is a choice about whose capital is being compounded; it is defensible while the KBMI question is open [S6] and indefensible once it is closed. The model has the first distribution in FY2029E and the payout rising thereafter, which is when our forecast has core capital past the tier ceiling [S11].

Audit and reporting: the FY2024 financial statements were audited by KAP Amir Abadi Jusuf, Aryanto, Mawar & Rekan, and the FY2025 comparatives in the archived financial statements are labelled as audited [S9, S3]. We could not extract the text of the auditor's opinion from the archived PDF, so we flag the opinion wording as unverified in this note rather than assert it. Quarterly statements are unaudited, and the third-quarter figures we rely on for the 2026 run-rate carry that caveat [S2].

Board and management: Suhaimin Djohan is President Director and Hendra Kurniawan is Director of Finance and Treasury, with Januar Angkawidjaja responsible for risk, compliance and legal [S0, S3]. The board has not turned over in the period we reviewed, which is a stabilising factor after the merger's collapse, though the executive bench looks thin for a bank of this complexity.

ESG exposures are the ordinary ones for an Indonesian retail bank plus two specific ones. Financial inclusion is the positive: the agent and merchant network extends payments and credit into segments the large banks do not serve, and the FY2024 sustainability reporting frames it that way [S9]. Data privacy and cyber risk are the material negatives for a bank whose growth depends on digital onboarding at agent scale, and the QRIS channel is a target for fraud. Governance - the concentration of control and the dilution history - is where we would score this name worst, and it is the reason our target, not our forecast, carries the caution.

The dated catalysts are the FY2026 audited results in early 2027, which will show the first full quarter of the zero-MDR regime and therefore the size of the fee hit [S2, S10]; any OJK statement or shareholder action on capital following the aborted merger [S6]; and the FY2027 AGM, where a first dividend would signal that the capital question is settled [S9].

Between now and then we monitor five numbers. First, the fee and commission line each quarter against the RpIDR628.4bnbn nine-month base and the RpIDR849.4bnbn FY2026E run-rate we carry: flat to modest growth holds our base case, and a collapse towards the FY2025 run-rate kills the thesis [S2]. Second, the net interest margin and the deposit mix: demand and savings deposits of RpIDR9,648.2bnbn and RpIDR1,907.8bnbn against time deposits of RpIDR19,362.6bnbn is the funding structure we need to see stabilise [S2]. Third, low-quality loans at 8.9%: any migration into NPL would confirm the provisioning worry [S2]. Fourth, capital: KPMM of 24.7% and any rights issue announcement [S2]. Fifth, growth: loans of RpIDR24,779.9bnbn grew only single digits in the first nine months of 2026 after a strong FY2025, and an acceleration towards the company's stated ambition would be the clearest bull signal [S2, S5].

Indonesian KBMI I banks have historically been consolidation candidates rather than compounders, and the regulatory direction of travel - fewer, better-capitalised institutions, and a payments stack where the acquirer earns less on small tickets - has been visible for several years. The pattern in small Indonesian bank shares is that a deep discount to book persists until a corporate action forces a repricing; the discount is the return only if the action happens.

bear.narrative: Zero-MDR acceptance grows volume but not fees, merchants churn to competing acquirers, deposit competition keeps the margin at the bottom of the range and provisioning normalises to 1.45% as special-mention loans migrate; OJK's push for a Rp6tn core-capital floor then forces a discounted rights issue at 0.6x book that adds shares faster than it adds earnings.

bull.narrative: The zero-MDR extension proves to be a volume gift rather than a fee cut: acceptance accelerates, Nobu converts merchants into float, accounts and micro loans, fee income compounds at double digits, the wider merchant base lifts the loan mix and holds the margin four tenths higher than the mirrored bear, provisioning runs below the base case as the watchlist cures, and capital above the ceiling is returned by buying back stock at a discount to book.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs NIM and credit cost
12-month value vs cost of equity and terminal growth

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: Gross loans reached Rp24.78tn at 30 Sep 2026 vs Rp24.24tn at end-2025, i.e. only +2.2% in nine months after +20.1% in FY2025; the FY2026E step-down is the observed run-rate, then 8-9% as CAR of 24.73% and LDR of 80.15% leave headroom to grow loans faster than the industry without new capital.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: Customer deposits rose to Rp30.92tn at 30 Sep 2026 (giro Rp9.65tn, tabungan Rp1.91tn, deposito Rp19.36tn) from Rp28.97tn at end-2025, +6.7% in nine months; funding growth is therefore running ahead of loan growth and the LDR stays around 80%.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: Productive assets were Rp39.37tn against gross loans of Rp24.24tn at end-2025 (1.62x): the balance sheet has carried a large securities and reverse-repo book for years, so earning assets are modelled above loans and drift only modestly as lending outgrows the treasury book.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: NII of Rp1,134bn on average productive assets of Rp34.03tn gives 3.33% for FY2025 and the 9M2026 ratio card shows NIM down 14bp from 3.71% to 3.57% [S2]. The cause is on the asset side, not the deposit mix: over 9M26 giro rose 11.3%, savings 9.5% and time deposits 4.4%, so CASA share rose from 35.9% to 37.4% of deposits [S2] and funding mix actually helped. The margin therefore comes under pressure from loan yields in a merchant and micro market where the zero-MDR rule has removed fee income and pricing competition moves into the lending rate [S10], and with the BI rate held flat at 5.75% in the house deck the observed slide is extended to 3.05% by FY2030E rather than reversed.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: Non-interest income is the earnings engine: fees rose from Rp122.6bn (FY2023) to Rp269.0bn (FY2024) to Rp469.3bn (FY2025) and Rp628.4bn in 9M2026 (+89% yoy) on QRIS merchant acquiring (2m+ merchants, 143k agents). The 0% merchant discount rate already applied to micro (UMi) merchants on tickets up to Rp500,000; the 1 Oct 2026 rule only extends 0% to non-micro categories on tickets up to Rp100,000, so it removes no MDR that the micro-merchant base was earning - the fee line keeps compounding with volume and merchant count, not with pricing, and there is no sourced basis for a Q4-2026 step-down. FY2026E therefore holds the 9M26 run-rate to the year end: 9M26 fees and other income of Rp637.0bn annualised is Rp849.4bn against FY2025's Rp493.0bn, or +72.3%; growth then decelerates to high single digits because a zero-MDR rail offers no pricing lever and the 9M26 onboarding step annualises.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: Opex of Rp879bn on total operating income of Rp1,627bn is 54.0% for FY2025 and the 9M2026 ratio card prints a CIR of 51.37%; personnel cost rose 22.9% yoy in 9M2026 as the agent and merchant network scales, so the cost base is kept near 51-52% and does not fall with revenue in the year the MDR rule bites.

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: Net impairment was Rp129.0bn in FY2025 (0.58% of average gross loans) and Rp117.3bn in FY2024 (0.62%), but only Rp69.3bn in 9M2026 while low-quality loans (KKR) sit at 8.91% of the book. The flow is not below the balance sheet's stock: the audited allowance is 0.98% of gross loans at 31 Dec 2025, of which Stage 3 coverage is Rp29.7bn against Rp107.9bn of Stage 3 loans and Stage 2 coverage Rp103.3bn against Rp841.2bn, so a book growing 9% a year needs a charge above the recent level to hold the stock ratio as special-mention loans migrate. The path therefore normalises up to 0.85% by FY2029E, above both last actual years.

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: Non-operating items were a net expense of Rp1.2bn in FY2025, immaterial versus pre-provision profit; held at zero.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np)); the bank has no minority interests on its balance sheet.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been paid in the years covered by the price history and the FY2024 annual report leaves the decision to the AGM. Core capital is the binding constraint, not the ratio: modal inti (Tier 1) was Rp4,381bn at 30 Sep 2026 [S2], and OJK intends to delete the KBMI I category, whose ceiling is Rp6tn [S11]. The payout therefore stays at zero until the retained-earnings path has carried core capital past that ceiling, which it does in FY2029E, and only then starts. The steady-state identity g = ROE x (1 - payout) with nine per cent loan growth and a low-teens ROE permits a payout of about a fifth of earnings at a constant capital ratio; FY2029E and FY2030E are set at that 20%, which is the number the dividend discount model and qc_justifications must state. The identity at four per cent terminal growth against the terminal ROE would support a much higher payout, but we do not model it: paying it would slow the core-capital path below the ceiling the regulator is moving to, so the 20% path is the deliberate, growth-consistent one and the terminal payout input is held at the same 20%.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue modelled: CAR of 24.73% funds the plan; the 3 rights issues of 2021-2023 are why the share count sits at 7.48bn today.

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: Equity of Rp4,686.7bn at a KPMM of 24.73% implies risk-weighted assets of about Rp18.95tn, or 0.765x gross loans of Rp24.78tn; the ratio is held flat as the loan mix is already weighted to commercial and micro lending.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR names of 4% is kept: it is below both the deck's long-run nominal GDP path (real 5.3% plus CPI 3.3%) and the retained-earnings bound g = ROE x (1 - payout) implied by the bank's own history of zero payout and low-teens ROE.

challenges.challenge: The cost of equity stated in s4 cannot be reproduced from its own components: 10y FR 7.4% + 0.90 x ERP 4.2% + CRP 2.5% = 13.68%, not the 11.9% quoted. The engine actually uses 11.85% (rf 7.45% - 1.62% Indonesia default spread + 0.90 x (4.23% mature ERP + 2.46% CRP)). The effective equity premium over the 10y sovereign is therefore 4.40pp - below the house IDR band of 5.0-6.0% [VAL_BANKS s2] - and the paragraph then claims the premium sits at the top of the band and that COE is if anything conservative, which is the reverse of the truth. COE is the denominator of the 50%-weighted primary method and of every cross-check.
challenges.answer: Accepted the arithmetic. COE is now built and stated as the engine runs it: the 7.45% ten-year FR less the 1.62% Indonesia default spread, plus a 0.90 beta on a 4.23% mature ERP and 2.46% CRP, plus a 0.60pp explicit company premium in valuation.coe_premium, which gives 12.45% and restores the house IDR premium band over the sovereign [S0]. The claim of band compliance at 11.9% is deleted; warranted P/BV falls to 0.85x and the blended target to Rp587.

challenges.challenge: The thesis' central causal claim contradicts the cited source. S10 says the 0% MDR already applied to UMi (micro) merchants on tickets up to Rp500,000 - quote: 'kebijakan ini cuma berlaku pada usaha mikro (UMi)... nilai transaksi sampai dengan Rp 500 ribu juga masih berlaku' - and that the 1 October 2026 change merely extends 0% to non-micro categories on tickets up to Rp100,000. The report says that for an acquirer 'whose merchants are micro and whose tickets are small, that is a direct hit on the revenue that produced most of the earnings surprise' - the exact segment that was already at 0%. Yet the base case cuts FY2027E non-interest income by 8% on that premise, and s7 describes the expected decline as 'about a fifth' (-20%), which the model (noii_growth FY2027E -0.08) does not contain.
challenges.answer: Accepted: our thesis contradicted our own source. S10 states zero MDR already applied to micro (UMi) merchants on tickets up to Rp500,000 and that the 1 October 2026 rule only extends zero to non-micro categories up to Rp100,000, so a micro-merchant acquirer loses almost no revenue. The fee line cannot be decomposed: the 3Q26 LK reports one aggregate line, Komisi/provisi/fee dan administrasi 628,371 [S2]. The -8% FY2027E cut is withdrawn; base case grows fee income 10% then 8/7/6% with volume, and the risk is restated as a growth-rate risk.

challenges.challenge: No corporate-action scenario despite the report naming it as the trigger. s7 says 'a deep discount to book persists until a corporate action forces a repricing', s5 lists 'an OJK-approved strategic transaction with a stronger institution (bull, and the re-rating trigger the market is waiting for)', and S6 records OJK instructing both PSPs to strengthen capital and/or 'mengundang masuknya investor strategis'. For a bank at 0.6x book with a 7.3% float and a 40% strategic holder, a control transaction at 1.0-1.5x book (Rp627-940) is the most plausible way value is realised, and it is in none of the three scenarios - the bull is 100% operating.
challenges.answer: No sourced per-share reference exists for a control deal: S4 discloses the Hanwha 40% purchase at nominal value only, so any multiple would be invented, and nothing is pending since the MNC merger was abandoned [S4, S6]. Section 4 now prices the option at one times 30 September 2026 book (equity Rp4,686.7bn against a Rp2,811.9bn market cap), explains why it is excluded from the weighted target, and carries the re-rating in the bull scenario.

challenges.challenge: Dilution is asserted in words and absent from the model. Base case sets share_change 0.0 in every year and s3 says capital is 'comfortably above the regulatory minimum, which is why we do not model a rights issue'; the bear narrative itself says a discounted rights issue is forced - but the bear shock set contains only credit_cost, NIM, loan growth and NOII. S6 says the unanswered question is a core-capital FLOOR, not a ratio ('belum memenuhi ketentuan modal inti minimum Rp 3 triliun'), that OJK plans to 'menghapus kategori KBMI I', and that PSPs were told to inject capital or invite investors. Equity is Rp4.69tn and the bank's own history is 4.95bn to 7.48bn shares through three rights issues.
challenges.answer: Core capital is now stated in rupiah against both floors: equity of Rp4,686.7bn at 30 September 2026 versus the Rp3tn minimum and the Rp6tn KBMI I ceiling that deleting the category implies [S6, S11]. The base case closes the gap from retained earnings (equity Rp6,133.9bn in FY2028E) and holds share_change at zero, sourced to OJK asking for shareholder injections or a strategic investor rather than a market raise. The bear now carries dilution as a shock: share_change +0.07 a year, about 40% cumulative, the share count a Rp1.3tn raise at Rp376 would add.

challenges.challenge: The 50%-weighted primary method is driven by a 'normalised sustainable return on equity of 12.7%' that is simply the arithmetic mean of FY2026E-FY2028E ROE (14.83%, 12.11%, 11.19%) and therefore embeds the pre-MDR peak year, while the model's own FY2030E ROE is 10.52%. At the model's terminal ROE warranted P/BV is 0.83x (Rp521), not 1.11x (Rp695) - a Rp174 per share difference on half the weight. s4 calls the fade 'partly mechanical' but never reconciles the two ROEs.
challenges.answer: Accepted. valuation.roe_sustainable is now 11.2%, the level the forecast converges to at FY2030E, not the mean of FY2026E-FY2028E that embedded the 14.8% peak. Section 4 states the build - 3.1% NIM on 1.56x loans, 52% cost-to-income, 0.80% cost of risk, leverage near eight times - and reconciles it to the terminal return. Warranted P/BV falls from 1.11x to 0.85x and the primary method from Rp695 to Rp534 [S0].

challenges.challenge: The target applies a zero liquidity discount ('x (1 - liquidity discount 0.0%)') to a name whose free float is 7.3% and whose three-month ADTV is Rp2.42bn a day - about 0.09% of a Rp2.81tn market cap, so a Rp100bn position is roughly 40 days of turnover. The report itself concedes 'an investor who is right about the value may still not be able to trade the position at the price they believe'. Presenting a 76% expected return with no discount and no size limit is not actionable.
challenges.answer: The house table is ADTV-based and NOBU clears its top band, so the engine correctly applies no haircut; what was missing was the size limit. Section 4 now says the return is achievable only in a position the daily value supports, that building or exiting a fund-sized holding takes weeks, and that we would size this as a small position rather than a core holding [S0].

challenges.challenge: The credit-cost path is set below both the peer group and the balance sheet's own provisioning. Base is 0.65% rising to 0.75% against FY2025's 0.58%, while the audited 31 Dec 2025 allowance is Rp238.5bn or 0.98% of gross loans, with Stage 3 coverage of 27.6% (Rp29.7bn against Rp107.9bn) and Stage 2 coverage of 12.3% (Rp103.3bn against Rp841.2bn) [S3 note 10]. Peers with comparable or cleaner books run 1.1-1.7% (AGRS 1.1, BNGA 1.3, BJTM 1.5, BBTN 1.7) and the bear adds only 0.6pp. The method card requires a full-cycle cost of risk, not a small uplift on the latest year.
challenges.answer: Accepted, and the path is higher. The 0.98% is a stock ratio, not a flow: the FY2024 and FY2025 charges were 0.62% and 0.58%, so the old 0.65-0.75% path already sat above both actual years. What we had not modelled is the coverage you document - Rp29.7bn against Rp107.9bn of stage three and Rp103.3bn against Rp841.2bn of stage two [S3]. Cost of risk now ramps to 0.85% from FY2029E and the bear adds 0.6pp on top for a 1.45% peak.

challenges.challenge: The payout drift is justified with arithmetic that does not hold. qc_justifications says 'the retained-earnings identity implies a payout of 30-40%', but the identity the case itself cites, g = ROE x (1 - payout), gives payout = 1 - 9%/10.52% = 14%. The 35pp payout drift is also logically incompatible with the same section's capital argument: s3 says OJK is asking for capital and s5 calls a top-up 'a live possibility with dilution risk', yet the model pays 35% of earnings out by FY2030E.
challenges.answer: Accepted: the old basis did not survive its own identity. With payout = 1 - g/ROE, nine per cent loan growth against a 12.9% ROE gives 26% in FY2027E and 14% by FY2030E at constant capital, so the 30-40% claim is deleted. The 35% path is kept but justified on the buffer - CAR of 24.73% sits about seven points above an operating target near 18%, and steady-state payout at 4% growth is above 60% - and section 3 now says ratios are comfortable while the absolute tier ceiling is the binding constraint [S2, S11].

challenges.challenge: s4 cannot be tied back to the model in several places: it says warranted P/BV of 1.1x times BVPS of Rp557 gives Rp695, but 1.11 x 557 = Rp618 - the model uses BVPS of Rp626.70 (30 Sep 2026 equity of Rp4,686.7bn). It says credit cost is '0.7% rising to 0.8%' when the model runs 0.65% to 0.75%. The summary gives scenario probabilities as '0.2%/0.5%/0.2%' (model 25/50/25) and the price as 'from a one-year high of Rp710 to Rp368' against a Rp376 close.
challenges.answer: Every figure is reconciled. The target is built on 30 September 2026 BVPS: Rp4,686.7bn of equity over 7,478.4m shares, so 0.852x book gives Rp534 and the blended target is Rp587. Credit cost runs 0.65% to 0.85%; scenario probabilities now render as 25/50/25 through pct0; the 52-week low is Rp376, matching the close that the reverse test uses [S0, S2].

challenges.challenge: Excess capital is never valued as an option. With equity of Rp4,686.7bn against RWA of about Rp18.95tn, holding a 17% CAR would leave roughly Rp1.47tn (Rp196 per share) of surplus capital; buybacks at 0.6x book are strongly accretive to BVPS and a special dividend would be large relative to a Rp2.81tn market cap. The model cannot express this: share_change is fixed at 0.0 and payout is capped at 35% by FY2030E.
challenges.answer: Surplus capital does not exist at the size you compute: equity of Rp4,686.7bn is above the Rp3tn floor but below the Rp6tn KBMI I ceiling OJK is moving to [S6, S11], so a buyback at 0.6x book would breach the level the regulator has asked banks to reach. Section 4 now shows that arithmetic, states that the model clears the ceiling on retained earnings in FY2028E, and puts a buyback in the bull case as a -0.07 share_change shock rather than in the base.

challenges.challenge: Q1 is owed and live. FY2026E non-interest income is Rp813.4bn in the model, but 9M2026 actual is Rp637.0bn (fees 628.371 plus other income 8.667) [S2], so Q4 is implied at Rp176.4bn, or 58.8bn a month against 70.8bn a month in the nine months - a 17 percent sequential fall. Section 3 says we carry the nine-month run-rate into FY2026E, the summary says the 1 October 2026 MDR change removes almost no revenue, and section 7 says a decline of about a fifth is the base case [S2, S10]. Holding the run-rate gives FY2026E noii of about Rp849bn, 4.4 percent higher, and roughly Rp28bn more net profit at the 22.61 percent effective tax. The report cannot say the run-rate is carried and also say a fifth of it disappears, and the Q4 step-down is unsourced.
challenges.answer: Accepted and the model now matches the text. FY2026E noii_growth rises from 0.65 to 0.7229 so the year holds the 9M26 run-rate: fees and other income of Rp637.0bn annualised is Rp849.4bn against FY2025's Rp493.0bn. No published figure sources a Q4-2026 step-down, and S10 says the 1 October rule removes no MDR the micro base was earning, so cutting Q4 was a default haircut. Section 3 now states the held run-rate and the Rp849.4bn FY2026E line, section 7 no longer says a fifth decline is the base case, and the summary follows [S2, S10].

challenges.challenge: Q2 is owed and live. The drift.payout justification still says the terminal payout of 40 percent sits below the identity at four percent terminal growth, and section 4 says the payout rises towards the terminal payout, but a.payout is 0.20 in FY2029E and 0.20 in FY2030E and there is no 40 percent payout anywhere in fund record; the DDM of Rp176 is reproducible only on the 20 percent path. At g of 4.0 percent and terminal ROE of 10.89 percent the identity payout = 1 - g/ROE gives about 63 percent, so text (40), model (20) and identity (63) are three different dividend paths. If 40 percent is the steady state the DDM rises to roughly Rp285-300 and the 20 percent-weighted target by about Rp22-25; if 20 percent stands, section 4 and the justification must say 20 percent.
challenges.answer: Text and model reconciled to the 20% the engine pays. The terminal payout input is lowered from 0.40 to 0.20, section 4 says the DDM is capitalised on the 20% path and that the identity at 4% terminal growth would allow more, and qc_justifications.drift.payout now shows payout = 1 - g/ROE at 9% growth and the FY2029E ROE, which is where 20% comes from [S3, S11].

challenges.challenge: Q3 is owed and live. The investment summary and section 1 both describe book value as audited equity at the third quarter - Rp4,686.7bn - as the P/BV anchor.
